errors.english: Thus what is remembered is non-different from what is to be proven,
errors.why: དྲན་བྱ is 'it should be recalled' (the earlier fault applies likewise); the reason is unestablished because, being non-different from the probandum, it cannot be stated, not that 'what is remembered' is non-different from it.
The verse introduced by དེ་ལ་བརྗོད་པ is a rejoinder that the author immediately rejects (འདི་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ), so it is not the author's own reply.

note: A sound rendering of a difficult Pramāṇa passage; two places where the argument's structure or speaker is blurred.
Faithful rendering of the apoha discussion with accurate technical terms.

errors.english: yet it is not merely an ordinary emanation
errors.why: The Tibetan says the mind-made body is to be seen as like an emanation but is not an emanation; 'merely an ordinary' softens the denial.

note: Accurate overall, with scripture citations correctly identified; inline Sanskrit/English doublets are only cosmetic.
Faithful translation of the body-as-cause-of-mind refutation, verses and commentary correctly separated.
Faithful word-commentary on the second-dhyāna similes; terms rendered correctly.

errors.english: A place for placing soil should be made around the latrine pit for the purpose of washing.
errors.why: རོལ་པོ is a vessel/item set down for washing, not soil (soil is ས, mentioned separately later).

note: A usable rendering of the latrine regulations; the terse rule-and-gloss structure is followed closely, with one doubtful object word.

errors.english: just as the sky cannot be a cause for production
errors.why: Space and the like are the example of causeless things, which are not produced at all; causeless arising is untenable, as with space.

errors.english: even suffering is defined in relation to the habituation of pleasure
errors.why: The Tibetan says suffering is produced (བྱས་པ) by the very habituation to pleasure, not 'defined in relation to' it.

errors.english: In the absence of true pleasure, one might perceive something as pleasurable that is actually neither pleasure nor pain.
errors.why: 'Its absence' refers to the absence of that (fear-habituation), and the cognition of pleasure arises toward suffering itself or toward the neutral; the English changes the referent and drops 'suffering itself' (and in the next clause drops 'pleasure').

note: Paraphrastic; the argument is broadly followed but the causeless-arising example is inverted and the closing analysis loses its referents.

errors.english: one must not repeatedly transport it upon the shoulders
errors.why: The commentary says that even a light load is not to be carried on shoulder, head or waist; there is no 'repeatedly' (the verse's ཡང་ཡང་ is 'even light', which the commentary glosses).

errors.english: One must avoid tying the edge of the lower robe in a knot.
errors.why: The rule, whose stated purpose is to keep the private parts covered, prescribes knotting the end of the lower robe when climbing a ladder or sleeping by day; the English (here and in the commentary) turns it into a prohibition.

note: A readable rendering of the deportment verses and commentary, but two rules are given wrongly in substance.

errors.english: will come to regard the essence as merely a perception
errors.why: སྙིང་པོའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཉེ་བར་འཇོག means they form the notion that there is an essence (sāra-saṃjñā), not that essence is a mere perception.

errors.english: the taught (Dharma) Buddhist teachings and natural law
errors.why: བསྟན་པའི་ཆོས is the Dharma of the teaching; 'and natural law' is not in the Tibetan.

errors.english: provides the pith instructions of the lineage for the purpose of abandoning
errors.why: རིགས here qualifies the instruction (the proper/appropriate instruction for abandoning), not a 'lineage'.

note: Generally accurate on the four truths, but the 'empty of the Omniscient One' gloss is misread and a few terms are padded.

errors.english: what kind of offense occurs when one takes ownership of requisites that have been carried off by another
errors.why: The requisites are the monk's own (བདག་གིར་བྱས་པ), carried off by a thief; the question is what offense arises in retrieving them, not in appropriating someone else's stolen goods.

errors.english: literally "an act that is not un-blameworthy,"
errors.why: ཁ་ན་མ་ཐོ་བ renders avadya, 'blameworthy act / fault'; the 'not un-blameworthy' etymology is misleading.

note: A sound rendering of the theft-analysis commentary, with one misread case relation and a confused gloss.
